meta.title: Where is Leonardo da Vinci buried? Amboise | Museum of Ages
meta.description: Leonardo da Vinci died at Cloux in Amboise on 2 May 1519. The church he was buried in is gone. What the chapel of Saint-Hubert holds, and how sure that is.

top.h1: Where is Leonardo da Vinci buried?
top.answer: Leonardo da Vinci died on 2 May 1519 at the manor of Cloux in Amboise, on the Loire in France, at 67. He had asked for a grave in Saint-Florentin, the church inside the royal château, and got it. Early in the 19th century that church was pulled down and the graves in it were broken up. Bones dug up on the site in 1863 lie today under a slab in the château's chapel of Saint-Hubert, and no one has yet proved that they are his.

paras: Francis I, the king of France, invited him. Leonardo had lived in Rome since 1513, and his patron there, Giuliano de' Medici, died in 1516. At Amboise they read that death as the reason he accepted. He left Rome in 1516 and came to Amboise, most likely in the autumn. The first note in his hand dated at Cloux is from May 1517.

He was 64. He brought his notebooks, his anatomy sheets and three paintings, which a visitor saw at the house a year later and which hang in the Louvre today. Francesco Melzi came with him, a young nobleman from Milan and his pupil, and so did his servant Battista de Vilanis. Salaì, his companion of many years, was in France for a time as well, but by 1518, the Louvre notes, he was living in Milan again.

The king gave him the manor of Cloux to live in, a short walk from the royal château, and a pension. Most sources put it at a thousand écus a year, the château's own site at 700. The will of 1519 gives his title in four words: painter to the King.

The house was not built for him. Étienne le Loup, a servant of Louis XI who had been raised to the nobility, built it in the later 1400s of brick and pale tuffeau stone. Charles VIII bought it, in 1490 the house says, and had a small chapel built. Louise of Savoy raised her children there, the house also says, among them the future Francis I. In Leonardo's day it was called Cloux. The name Clos Lucé came later.

It still stands, a listed monument since 1862. The family that has owned it since 1854 restored it from 1954 on, to show it as he may have known it. The walls and the dovecote are old. What you see inside is a presentation: the furniture, and the room shown as his bedroom, are the house's choices, since no document names his room. The house attributes the painted Annunciation in the chapel to pupils of his workshop. That is the house's view, not a proven fact.

paras: On 10 October 1517 a cardinal came to see him. Luigi d'Aragona was travelling through France with his secretary, Antonio de Beatis, and after a midday meal at Tours they rode on to Amboise. De Beatis kept a diary. His entry for that day is why the wing shows this day of all days.

What he wrote, in short. Leonardo was old, over seventy he guessed, though he was 65. He showed the cardinal three pictures: a portrait of a Florentine lady painted for Giuliano de' Medici, a young Saint John the Baptist, and the Virgin and Child in the lap of Saint Anne. Today they are taken to be the Louvre's Mona Lisa, Saint John and Saint Anne, though the diary names no Mona Lisa. Part of his right hand was paralysed, so no more good painting could be expected from him. But he still drew, and he taught, and a Milanese pupil of his worked well. He said he had dissected more than thirty bodies, men and women of every age, and he showed volumes of his writings on anatomy, on water and on machines, all in Italian.

blocks.h: What he worked on in France
paras: He did not stop working. His notes show him at Romorantin, south of Orléans, where he designed a palace for the king, with canals to join it to the Loire. It was never built. Francis I built Chambord instead. He put on feasts for the court, and the château places him at the centre of the celebrations at Amboise in the spring of 1518, while saying its archives on that are thin. The house counts four feasts, one of them in front of Cloux. That is the house's own account.

He kept drawing. The deluge drawings at Windsor are dated about 1517 to 1518, and you can open one of them in the wing, under the study window. A sheet of geometry carries, Treccani notes, the date 24 June 1518 and a note that it was written at the palace of Cloux. Museo Galileo says he went back to sorting his notes, probably with a book in mind. And he was still at the Saint Anne: the last brushstrokes on her dress came to light in the restoration of 2010 to 2012, the Louvre reports.

blocks.h: His will, and the day he died
paras: On 23 April 1519 he made his will at Cloux, before a royal notary of Amboise. The original is lost and the text survives in copies. The date on it reads 1518, before Easter: the year then turned at Easter, so by our reckoning it is 1519. He wanted his grave in Saint-Florentin, the castle church at Amboise, and asked that its chaplains carry him there, with sixty poor men bearing sixty candles, masses in the churches of the town, and alms for the poor of its two hospitals.

Francesco Melzi, named his only executor, got all his books, the instruments and pictures of his trade, his clothes at Cloux and what was still owed of his pension. Battista de Vilanis got half of a garden Leonardo owned outside the walls of Milan, a water right there, and the furniture and household goods at Cloux. Salaì got the other half of the garden, where he had already built himself a house. The maid Maturina got a good black cloak lined with fur, a length of cloth and two ducats. His half-brothers in Florence got the money he had on deposit there. No painting is named. The three pictures the cardinal saw are not in the will at all, and the Louvre's reading is that the king had very probably bought them in 1518, through a payment to Salaì.

He died nine days later, on 2 May 1519, at Cloux. He was 67. The record of it is a letter: on 1 June Melzi wrote to Leonardo's brothers in Florence that he had died on 2 May with all the rites of the Church. What he died of, nobody wrote down. Vasari, decades later, says he had been ill for many months. The paralysed hand of 1517 is often put down to a stroke, and a medical paper of 2019 argued for nerve damage instead. Both are readings. There is no record.

The story everyone knows goes like this. The king, who often visited him, came in. Leonardo sat up in bed to speak of his illness, a last fit took him, and he died in the king's arms. Vasari told it first in 1550, in the first edition of his Lives, 31 years after the death, and told it again in 1568. In the same breath he gave Leonardo's age as 75. He was 67.

Most historians doubt the scene, for two reasons. Royal acts of 1 and 3 May 1519 are dated at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, near Paris, where the court was celebrating the birth of the king's second son. And Melzi's letter, written at Amboise a month after the death, says nothing of the king. The doubt is not new: scholars raised it in the early 1800s. It is not proof either. An act is dated where the chancery sits, and could be issued without the king's own hand, so the acts make his presence near Paris very likely, no more. The scene cannot be ruled out. It is just that no record puts the king in the room.

Painters made the scene famous. François-Guillaume Ménageot showed a large canvas of it at the Paris Salon of 1781, and that picture, the Bibliothèque nationale de France says, is what fixed the story in the public mind. It hangs today in the king's bedchamber of the Château royal d'Amboise, the same château that holds the grave. Ingres painted the scene again in 1818, in Rome, on a small canvas of about 40 by 50 centimetres, now in the Petit Palais in Paris. The Petit Palais's own record calls the episode most likely invented, and notes that Ingres took the king's face from a portrait by Titian painted twenty years after the death. The wing hangs a reproduction of the Ingres in its grave court, enlarged, and its label says what the picture is: a scene imagined three centuries later.

pic.title: The king at the bedside, as Ingres imagined it
pic.what: a reproduction of the painting of 1818 by Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, as the wing hangs it, enlarged, in the grave court. The scene is Vasari's story, painted three centuries after the death.
pic.alt: A dying old man with a long white beard lies in a bed, held up by a young king in rich dress, with courtiers around them in a dark room. A reproduction of the painting of 1818 by Ingres.

paras: He was buried in Saint-Florentin, as his will had asked. The church stood inside the walls of the royal château. On what day, nobody knows for sure. The date often given, 12 August 1519, rests on a register entry known only from a copy that surfaced after 1863, and Arsène Houssaye, who printed it, said himself that it must be taken with the greatest reserve.

Early in the 19th century the church was pulled down. The château belonged then to a senator of Napoleon. The tombstones were sold and the lead coffins melted, Houssaye wrote some fifty-five years later, and the bones lay about until the château's gardener gathered them and buried them near where the choir had been. The ground was raised by two or three metres and planted. So the graves were already broken up before anyone went looking for his.

In 1863 Houssaye, a writer with the emperor's backing, dug on the site. On 20 August his workers opened an old tomb in the choir, against the wall, under rough stones left from the demolition. In it lay a skeleton with its head on one hand, a silver coin of the young Francis I, scraps of brown wool and the remains of sandals. In the rubble near it, turned over more than once, they found pieces of stone with letters cut into them: INC, LEO, and three that together read EO DUS VINC. Doctors told him the skull was that of a man of about seventy. Houssaye compared the skull with a portrait, measured the skeleton and believed he had found Leonardo. He also wrote that at that moment nobody dared to say so.

The bones he chose were reburied in the chapel of Saint-Hubert, the small late Gothic chapel on the château's ramparts, in 1874, the château says. A marble bust set up in the gardens in 1869 marks the first grave. In the chapel a floor slab carries his name. The slab was remade in 1930, the château says, and in the 2000s a bronze medallion with his profile, by the sculptor Jean Cardot, was added.

How sure can anyone be? Not very. The identification rests on what one man read in 1863: a tomb in the right place, a coin of the right reign, a skull that seemed to fit, and letters found loose in rubble, to which he himself gave only a supporting role. The French state's heritage record for the château says the chapel would contain his remains, in the conditional (contiendrait). The tourist office of Amboise calls them presumed remains. A research project has been looking since 2016 for DNA to compare them with, Smithsonian magazine reported in January 2026, and has nothing certain yet. So the honest answer to where he is buried: in the chapel of Saint-Hubert at Amboise, most likely, and nobody can prove it.

Our Leonardo wing rebuilds the house at Cloux in code, from plans and photographs, on the day of the cardinal's visit, 10 October 1517. The time of day is ours. You go into one room, the great hall, with a fireplace in the style of about 1500 and furniture of the kind such a house had then, none of it his. The small chapel, the study and the north room stay views from outside. The wing puts the visit behind the study window, which is a guess, since the diary names no room. Which room was his bedroom is the real house's proposal, not a record.

The grave court at the end of the walk is the museum's own place, not the chapel at Amboise. Its slab with his name, its model of the low sun of 2 May 1519 at a minute we chose, and its stone with the year of the dig are made for the exhibition. The stop is called Presumed, for the reason this page gives. Then it gets dark, and the stars stand as they stood over Cloux that evening in October 1517.

blocks.intro: The page relies on Leonardo's will of 1519 and Antonio de Beatis' diary of 1517 in their printed editions, Vasari's Lives of 1550 and 1568, the catalogue of the acts of Francis I, Melzi's letter of 1 June 1519 as printed in 1804, Arsène Houssaye's account of his dig of 1863, and the records and pages of the Louvre, the Treccani biographical dictionary, the Château du Clos Lucé, the Château royal d'Amboise, the Bibliothèque nationale de France, the French Ministry of Culture's heritage records, the Petit Palais, Museo Galileo and Smithsonian magazine, all read on 13 October 2026.

blocks.h: See the house in the wing
blocks.p: This door opens the walk at his last house. It goes through the yard into the great hall, past the chapel and the study window, and ends in the grave court, under the stars of that evening.
